probes.question: What did the rare bounced-back particles show about atoms?
options: Atoms are solid balls all the way through
A tiny central nucleus holds most of the atom's mass, with empty space around it
Electrons are heavier than the nucleus

probes.question: True or false: Geiger and Marsden's experiment used a very thin gold foil.

image.alt: A 3D computer rendering of the Geiger-Marsden apparatus with a gold foil target, screen and rotating disc.

panels.text: Manchester, 1909. In Ernest Rutherford's lab, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fire alpha particles from radium at a very thin gold foil and count flashes on a screen.
The popular atom model predicted that the particles should all go almost straight through.
But about 1 in 8000 bounced back. Rutherford said it was as unlikely as a huge shell fired at tissue paper coming back to hit you.
His explanation: an atom has a tiny, dense centre holding most of its mass. Most particles sail past it through the empty space around it, and rare near-hits scatter them.
